sourceReview: Read bundled BSB Psalm 82 in full with each verse's related passages before drafting. References are thematic or literary comparisons, not an invented historical occasion. Scripture is never stored in the notes; it loads from the bundled BSB.

study.title: God judges the judges
study.intro: Asaph pictures God standing in the heavenly council, rebuking unjust rulers, commanding justice for the weak, and finally calling on God to judge the whole earth.
study.context: Psalm 82 is headed 'A Psalm of Asaph.' It is a courtroom scene. God presides over an assembly of 'gods,' and charges them with failing to defend the poor and fatherless. Interpreters differ on whether these 'gods' are human judges who carried God's authority or spiritual powers over the nations; either way, they are accountable and mortal. Jesus quoted verse 6 in John 10:34. The psalm ends with a prayer for God Himself to rise and judge every nation.
study.peopleNote: The heading names Asaph, the Levite worship leader appointed by David; the app has no Asaph profile yet. Jesus quotes verse 6 in John 10, so Jesus is linked. Planned paintings would show courts, gates and the needy; God is never portrayed as a human body.

verses.title: The divine assembly
verses.heading: God takes His seat as Judge
verses.meaning: The heading names Asaph. The scene opens: 'God presides in the divine assembly; He renders judgment among the gods.' God stands or sits as the presiding Judge over a council. Those called 'gods' are powerful beings or rulers who held authority under Him. No power, earthly or spiritual, is beyond His oversight. The psalm wants every person with authority to remember that they will stand before the true Judge.
verses.context: 1 Kings 22:19 describes the LORD sitting on His throne with the host of heaven around Him. Job 1:6 speaks of the sons of God presenting themselves before the LORD. Exodus 21:6 uses the word 'God' (elohim) where many translate 'judges.'
explore: Divine assembly
A council gathered before God, pictured as His court where He rules and gives verdicts.
Gods
Here elohim, a word used for mighty beings or for human judges acting with God-given authority.
verses.reflect: How does knowing that every authority answers to God shape the way you view those in power?
verses.alt: A grand stone court hall stands empty and bright, with a raised seat bathed in light.

verses.title: How long will you judge unjustly?
verses.heading: The charge of corruption
verses.meaning: Verse 2 brings the accusation: 'How long will you judge unjustly and show partiality to the wicked?' The rulers have twisted justice, siding with the powerful and guilty. 'How long' shows God's patience is running out. Partiality means favoring someone because of status or bribes. 'Selah' asks the reader to pause over the seriousness of injustice in God's eyes. God takes unfair courts personally.
verses.context: Deuteronomy 1:17 tells judges, 'Do not show partiality in judgment; hear both small and great alike.' Leviticus 19:15 forbids favoring the poor or deferring to the great. James 2:1 warns believers not to show favoritism.
explore: Partiality
Literally 'lifting up faces,' showing favor because of who someone is rather than what is right.
Unjustly
With injustice or perversion of what is right, especially in legal decisions.
verses.reflect: Where might you be tempted to show favoritism, and how could you act more fairly?
verses.alt: A wealthy man hands a coin purse to an official at a city gate while a poor woman waits.

verses.title: Defend the fatherless
verses.heading: What justice requires
verses.meaning: Verse 3 states the duty: 'Defend the cause of the weak and fatherless; uphold the rights of the afflicted and oppressed.' True rulers protect those who cannot protect themselves. Orphans, the poor and the crushed were often ignored by courts. God names them first. Justice is not neutral indifference but active defense of the vulnerable. This command applies to anyone with influence over others.
verses.context: Deuteronomy 10:18 says God executes justice for the fatherless and the widow. Isaiah 1:17 commands, 'Defend the fatherless and plead the case of the widow.' James 1:27 calls caring for orphans and widows pure religion.
explore: Fatherless
Children without a father to protect and provide for them, among the most vulnerable in ancient society.
Afflicted
Those who are bowed down by poverty, suffering or mistreatment, with little power to help themselves.
verses.reflect: Who around you is weak or overlooked, and how could you stand up for them?
verses.alt: A young orphan boy and his grandmother stand at a village gate where an elder listens kindly.

verses.title: Rescue the needy
verses.heading: Snatch them from the wicked
verses.meaning: Verse 4 adds urgency: 'Rescue the weak and needy; save them from the hand of the wicked.' The verbs are strong: rescue and save. The vulnerable are pictured in the grip of predators. Judges were meant to be deliverers, pulling people free. God's standard is not just avoiding harm but intervening to stop it. Those with power will answer for whether they used it to help.
verses.context: Proverbs 24:11 says, 'Rescue those being led away to death.' Job 29:12 recalls Job rescuing the poor who cried for help. Jeremiah 22:3 commands, 'Rescue the victim of robbery from the hand of his oppressor.'
explore: Needy
Those who lack basic necessities and depend on others' kindness or justice.
Hand of the wicked
A picture of the power and control of evil people over their victims.
verses.reflect: Is there a situation where God may be asking you to step in and help someone in need?
verses.alt: A traveler pulls a man up from a ditch at the side of a rocky road.

verses.title: Wandering in darkness
verses.heading: Foundations shaken
verses.meaning: Verse 5 describes the corrupt rulers: 'They do not know or understand; they wander in the darkness; all the foundations of the earth are shaken.' Their injustice comes from willful blindness. Without God's light they stumble. When those meant to uphold justice fail, the whole order of society trembles. Justice is like a foundation; remove it and everything built on it is unsteady.
verses.context: Psalm 11:3 asks, 'When the foundations are destroyed, what can the righteous do?' Proverbs 4:19 says the way of the wicked is like deep darkness. John 3:19 says people loved darkness rather than light.
explore: Foundations
The base on which a building stands; here the moral order of justice that holds society together.
Darkness
A picture of ignorance, sin and moral confusion apart from God's truth.
verses.reflect: Where do you need God's light to help you see clearly and act rightly?
verses.alt: Cracked stone walls and a tilted gateway stand in dim twilight after an earthquake.

verses.title: You are gods
verses.heading: A high calling
verses.meaning: Verse 6 recalls their status: 'I have said, You are gods; you are all sons of the Most High.' God had given these rulers dignity and authority under Him. Jesus quoted this line in John 10 when accused of blasphemy, arguing that if Scripture calls those who received God's word 'gods,' He, sent by the Father, may rightly be called God's Son. High rank, however, means greater accountability.
verses.context: John 10:34-35 records Jesus saying, 'Is it not written in your Law: I have said you are gods?' Exodus 22:28 says not to curse God or the rulers of your people. Romans 13:1 teaches that authorities are established by God.
explore: Sons of the Most High
A title of honor for those given authority under God, reflecting His rule.
Most High
A name for God emphasizing He is above every other power or ruler.
verses.reflect: How does the dignity God has given you increase your responsibility to act justly?
verses.alt: Robed elders sit on stone benches at a city gate with scrolls in their laps.

verses.title: Like mortals you will die
verses.heading: The fall of the mighty
verses.meaning: Verse 7 delivers the verdict: 'But like mortals you will die, and like rulers you will fall.' Their high titles will not save them. Like every human, they will die; like many proud princes, they will be toppled. Power is temporary and borrowed. God alone is eternal. This sentence humbles everyone tempted to think position puts them above accountability.
verses.context: Isaiah 14:12 describes the fall of a proud ruler: 'How you have fallen from heaven!' Psalm 146:3-4 says not to trust in princes, for their plans perish when they die. Ezekiel 28:9 asks a king if he will still say 'I am a god' before his killers.
explore: Mortals
Human beings subject to death; the word stresses weakness and limits.
Fall
To be brought down from power, defeated or dying, losing all status.
verses.reflect: How does remembering that all human power is temporary change what you put your trust in?
verses.alt: A toppled stone throne lies in ruins among weeds in an abandoned palace courtyard.

verses.title: Arise, O God
verses.heading: The prayer for true justice
verses.meaning: Verse 8 ends with Asaph's prayer: 'Arise, O God, judge the earth, for all the nations are Your inheritance.' After seeing corrupt rulers condemned, the psalmist asks God Himself to take over. Every nation belongs to Him. This is a prayer for God's kingdom to come with perfect justice. Christians see its answer in Jesus, to whom the nations are given and who will judge the world in righteousness.
verses.context: Psalm 2:8 says, 'Ask Me, and I will make the nations Your inheritance.' Acts 17:31 says God has set a day when He will judge the world in righteousness by the Man He has appointed. Revelation 11:15 announces that the kingdom of the world has become the kingdom of our Lord.
explore: Arise
A call for God to stand up and act, as a judge rising to give verdict or a warrior to fight.
Inheritance
Rightful possession passed down; here every nation belongs to God as His own.
verses.reflect: What injustice in the world would you like to bring to God in prayer, asking Him to arise?
verses.alt: Morning light spreads across a wide landscape of many distant villages and hills.
